Define Model Covariates from Raster Layers

Source: R/scale_vars.R
msr_vars.Rd

These helpers declare how each model covariate is computed from a source raster layer, and whether its scale is estimated or fixed. Use kernel_var() for a kernel-weighted mean, landscape_var() for a landscape metric of a categorical raster, and surface_var() for a texture metric of a continuous raster. Collect the specifications with msr_vars() and pass the result to the scale_vars argument of kernel_prep() and kernel_scale.raster().

The helpers are optional. Without scale_vars, kernel_prep() turns each raster layer into one kernel-weighted mean covariate with the layer's name.

Usage

msr_vars(...)

kernel_var(source)

landscape_var(
  source,
  metric,
  radius = NULL,
  base = exp(1),
  classes_max = NULL,
  class = NULL
)

surface_var(source, metric, radius = NULL, weighted = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_vars'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

...

For msr_vars(), one or more named specifications created with kernel_var(), landscape_var(), or surface_var(). Each name becomes the covariate's column name in the model data. Names must be unique, and "x" is reserved for internal coordinate data. At least one specification is required. For print(), further arguments passed to base::print.data.frame().

source

Character scalar. Name of the source layer in the raster_stack given to kernel_prep(). It must match a layer name exactly. Several covariates can share one source.

metric

Character scalar. Code of the metric to compute within the buffer, matched case-insensitively. landscape_var() accepts the 25 landscape metrics and surface_var() the six surface metrics defined in Details.

radius

Optional positive numeric scalar. Buffer radius in map units. With the default NULL, the radius is estimated with the model. It is a hard radius, so it has no Hessian standard error (see multiScaleR-kernels). When supplied, the metric is computed once at this radius and enters the model as an ordinary covariate, with no scale to estimate. Keep it within the max_D of kernel_prep(), because cells beyond max_D are never extracted.

base

Positive numeric scalar, not equal to 1. Base of the logarithm used by Shannon diversity ("shdi") and the information-theory metrics ("ent", "condent", "joinent", "mutinf"). Default: exp(1), so entropies are in nats. Use 2 for bits, which reproduces FRAGSTATS and the landscapemetrics package for the information-theory metrics, or 10 for Hartleys. The base cancels in the ratio metrics ("shei", "contag", "iji", "relmutinf"). The modified Simpson metrics ("msidi", "msiei") always use the natural log, as FRAGSTATS and landscapemetrics define them. For these and for metrics that take no logarithm, landscape_var() warns and ignores a non-default base.

classes_max

Positive numeric scalar. Number of classes that could occur in the landscape. Required for relative patch richness ("rpr"), where it is the denominator, and unused by every other metric. The observed class count is never substituted, so landscape_var() stops if "rpr" is requested without it.

class

Optional integer-like scalar. The focal class code for the class-level metrics ("clumpy", "pland", "ca"), which describe one class rather than the whole buffer. It must match one of the class codes in the source raster. It is required for those three metrics and an error for every other metric.

weighted

Logical, for surface_var() only. With FALSE (default), the metric summarizes every cell within a hard-edged circle, and the estimated scale is that radius. With TRUE, each cell is weighted by the model's distance kernel (the kernel given to kernel_prep()) and the estimated scale is the kernel's sigma, as for a kernel-weighted mean. Gaussian, negative exponential, and exponential power weights change smoothly with sigma, so sigma gets a standard error. With kernel = "fixed" the weights are 1 or 0, so the covariate is again a hard radius without a standard error. Weighting applies only to the distribution metrics ("sa", "sq", "ssk", "sku"), not to "sdq" or "sdr", and requires radius = NULL.

x

A multiScaleR_vars object returned by msr_vars().

Value

msr_vars() returns a data frame of class c("multiScaleR_vars", "data.frame") with one row per covariate and these columns:

  • covariate: the name given in ....

  • source: the source raster layer.

  • type: "kernel", "landscape", or "surface".

  • metric: the metric code, or NA for a kernel mean.

  • radius: the fixed radius in map units, or NA when the scale is estimated.

  • optimize: TRUE when the scale is estimated with the model.

  • weighted: TRUE for a kernel-weighted surface metric.

  • base: the logarithm base actually used.

  • classes_max: the denominator of "rpr", or NA.

  • class: the focal class of a class-level metric, or NA.

kernel_var(), landscape_var(), and surface_var() each return a list of class "multiScaleR_var" holding one specification. Pass it to msr_vars(). It has no use on its own.

print() displays the specification table and returns x invisibly.

Choose a covariate type

HelperSource rasterWhat it summarizesScale
kernel_var()Any numeric layerKernel-weighted mean of the cell valuesSigma, estimated, with a standard error
landscape_var()Categorical, with integer class codesComposition, edges, aggregation, information theory, or one focal classHard radius, estimated without a standard error, or fixed
surface_var()Continuous, such as elevation or canopy heightVariation, distribution shape, slope, or reliefHard radius (estimated or fixed), or sigma with weighted = TRUE

A kernel mean describes how much of something surrounds a point. Landscape and surface metrics describe how it is arranged or how much it varies, so they complement the mean rather than replace it. Note that for a metric, changing the radius changes both the spatial scale and the statistical quantity summarized. Landscape metrics require finite, integer-like class codes, and both metric types require square raster cells.

Whether a scale is a smooth kernel width or a hard radius decides how it can be estimated and reported. multiScaleR-kernels explains the difference, and why a hard radius has a stepped likelihood and no Hessian standard error.

Combine covariate types

One msr_vars() call can mix all three types, including several covariates from the same source layer. For example, a kernel-weighted mean of forest cover and a fixed-radius edge density of the same layer:

vars <- msr_vars(
  forest_mean  = kernel_var("forest"),
  forest_ed500 = landscape_var("forest", metric = "ed", radius = 500)
)
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts, rasters, max_D = 1000,
                             scale_vars = vars)

A covariate with a fixed radius is computed once and is not re-evaluated during optimization, which can save considerable time. Under kernel = "expow", a hard-radius covariate does not use the kernel shape. Its reported shape and shape standard error are NA, and its unused shape position is left out of model-selection parameter counts.

Not every fitting route accepts every covariate type. Kernel means, weighted "sq", and fixed-radius metrics work with every route, including the analytic backends of multiScale_optim() and multiScale_bayes(), within each route's kernel restrictions. Those routes need a Gaussian or negative exponential kernel for weighted "sq". An estimated hard radius, and any weighted metric other than "sq", needs the default refit backend. See multiScaleR-fitting-methods and vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR") for the full feature table.

Landscape metric definitions

Each landscape metric summarizes the cells whose centers lie within the radius. In the formulas, n is the number of valid (non-missing) cells, n_i the number in class i, p_i = n_i / n, m the number of classes present, res the cell size in map units, and A = n * res^2 / 10000 the buffer area (hectares when map units are meters). g_ij counts pairs of cells that share a side, have classes i and j, and both lie in the buffer. Each pair is counted in both directions, and q_ij = g_ij / sum(g). Logarithms use base where marked, and the natural log otherwise.

Composition (how many classes, and how evenly they share the buffer):

CodeNameDefinitionUnits or range
shdiShannon diversity-sum(p_i * log(p_i)), with baseLog units, 0 or more
sheiShannon evennessshdi / log(m), with base. 0 when m = 10 to 1
sidiSimpson diversity1 - sum(p_i^2)0 to 1
sieiSimpson evennesssidi / (1 - 1 / m). NA when m = 10 to 1
msidiModified Simpson diversity-log(sum(p_i^2))Natural log units, 0 or more
msieiModified Simpson evennessmsidi / log(m). Undefined when m = 10 to 1
prPatch richnessmNumber of classes
prdPatch richness densitym / A * 100Classes per 100 ha
rprRelative patch richnessm / classes_max * 100Percent
taTotal areaAHectares

Edge (how much boundary separates different classes). Here E is the number of cell sides shared by two buffer cells of different classes, and B the number of cell sides on the buffer's outer boundary or next to a missing cell:

CodeNameDefinitionUnits or range
teTotal edgeE * resMap units (meters)
edEdge densityE * res / AMeters per hectare
lsiLandscape shape index(E + B) / Pmin(n), where Pmin(n) is the smallest possible perimeter, in cell sides, of n cellsRatio, 1 or more

Aggregation (whether cells of a class sit together or are mixed with other classes):

CodeNameDefinitionUnits or range
pladjProportion of like adjacenciessum(g_ii) / sum(g) * 100Percent
aiAggregation indexsum(p_i * (g_ii / 2) / gmax_i) * 100, where gmax_i is the most like adjacencies n_i cells can havePercent
contagContagion(1 + sum(q_ij * log(q_ij)) / (2 * log(m))) * 100. NA when m < 20 (interspersed) to 100 (one class)
ijiInterspersion and juxtaposition-sum(e * log(e)) / log(m * (m - 1) / 2) * 100, where e is each class pair's share of the adjacencies between different classes. NA when m < 3 or no such adjacencies existNear 0 (one pair dominates) to 100 (all pairs equally adjacent)

Information theory (pattern complexity, split into composition and configuration, following Nowosad and Stepinski 2019). With q_i = sum_j(q_ij):

CodeNameDefinitionUnits or range
entMarginal entropy, H(x)-sum(q_i * log(q_i)), with baseLog units. Rises with the number and evenness of classes
joinentJoint entropy, H(x, y)-sum(q_ij * log(q_ij)), with baseLog units. Total complexity of the pattern
condentConditional entropy, H(y given x)joinent - entLog units. Uncertainty about a neighbor's class given a cell's class
mutinfMutual information, I(y, x)ent - condentLog units. How much a cell's class tells you about its neighbor's
relmutinfRelative mutual informationmutinf / ent, and 1 when mutinf = 00 to 1, unaffected by base

Both clumping and regular alternation make neighbors predictable and raise mutinf. Its size also depends on ent, so it is not a composition-free aggregation index. relmutinf rescales it so that configuration can be compared across buffers with different composition.

Class level (one focal class k, set with class):

CodeNameDefinitionUnits or range
plandPercentage of landscapen_k / n * 100. 0 when the class is absentPercent
caClass arean_k * res^2 / 10000. 0 when the class is absentHectares
clumpyClumpiness indexWith G = g_kk / (4 * n_k - Pmin(n_k)) and P = n_k / n: (G - P) / (1 - P) when G >= P or P >= 0.5, otherwise (G - P) / P, the FRAGSTATS definition. NA when the class is absent or fills the bufferUnitless, from -1 (maximally dispersed) through 0 (random) to 1 (maximally clumped). landscapemetrics 2.2.1 divides by -P in the second case, which reverses the sign of dispersed classes

Surface metric definitions

Each surface metric summarizes the values z of the n valid cells whose centers lie within the radius. s is the sample standard deviation ("sq") and res the cell size in map units.

CodeNameDefinitionUnits
saAverage roughnesssum(abs(z - mean(z))) / nRaster units
sqRoot mean square roughnesssqrt(sum((z - mean(z))^2) / (n - 1)). NA when n < 2Raster units
sskSkewnesssqrt(n * (n - 1)) / (n - 2) * (sum((z - mean(z))^3) / n) / s^3. NA when n < 3 or s = 0Unitless. Positive when a few high values stand out
skuExcess kurtosis(sum((z - mean(z))^4) / n) / s^4 - 3. NA when s = 0Unitless. 0 for normally distributed values
sdqRoot mean square slopeSquare root of the mean of ((z - z_right)^2 + (z - z_below)^2) / res^2 over cells whose right and lower neighbors are both in the bufferRaster units per map unit
sdrSurface area ratio(sum(a) / (k * res^2) - 1) * 100, where a is the three-dimensional area of each of the k blocks of 2 x 2 cell centers in the bufferPercent

"sa", "sq", "ssk", and "sku" match the geodiv package. "sdq" is a true slope (rise over run). geodiv::sdq() assumes a cell spacing of 1, so it equals "sdq" multiplied by res. "sdr" uses the real values and cell size, so a plane tilted at slope t returns (sqrt(1 + t^2) - 1) * 100. geodiv::sdr() rescales the surface to a unit range first, so its values differ. Read "sdq" and "sdr" as a slope and an area ratio only when the raster values and the map share units, as elevation in meters does.

Kernel-weighted surface metrics

With weighted = TRUE, each cell gets the kernel weight w = w(d) of its distance d from the point (see multiScaleR-kernels), using the cells extracted within max_D. With the weighted mean mu = sum(w * z) / sum(w):

CodeWeighted definition
sasum(w * abs(z - mu)) / sum(w)
sqsqrt(sum(w * (z - mu)^2) / sum(w)), and 0 for constant values
ssk(sum(w * (z - mu)^3) / sum(w)) / sq^3. NA when sq = 0
sku(sum(w * (z - mu)^4) / sum(w)) / sq^4 - 3. NA when sq = 0

Weighted "sq" divides by the sum of weights, so it is a population-style spread and differs from the n - 1 form of the unweighted metric. The weighted skewness and kurtosis use plain standardized moments, without the small-sample adjustment of the unweighted "ssk". Weighted "sq" is smooth in sigma except where the weighted spread is zero. Absolute deviations ("sa") and the standardized higher moments have additional points where they are not smooth or not defined. Within one evaluation, weighted metrics reuse weights and centered moments only when their source, scale, shape, and valid cells match exactly. Their scales are still estimated separately. Under kernel = "fixed", the fitted scale is a hard cutoff radius. It has no standard error or Wald limits, although the weighted definitions above still apply.

Check a metric before you optimize it

Before estimating the radius of "iji", "siei", or "msiei", inspect a pilot kernel_prep() result or a few fixed radii. These metrics can be undefined or nearly constant when buffers hold too few classes, too few adjacencies between different classes, or nearly identical evenness at every point. "iji" in particular returns NA with fewer than three classes, and small buffers can make it NA everywhere. If so, use a larger radius, increase max_D, or choose a more stable diversity, entropy, or edge metric. A candidate scale that leaves a covariate undefined at a modeled observation is rejected during optimization, so every candidate is compared on the same observations.

The adjacency and information-theory metrics accept a limited number of classes, which guards against passing a continuous raster by mistake and keeps raster projection times bounded. The limits are 200 classes for the like-adjacency metrics ("ai", "pladj", "clumpy") and 50 for the metrics built from the full class-pair table ("contag", "iji", and the information-theory metrics), whose cost grows with the square of the class count.

During optimization, the adjacency metrics reuse sorted cell and neighbor-pair distances instead of rescanning every buffered cell at each radius, and metrics on the same source and radius share their counts. This saves time at the cost of retained memory, which estimate_multiscale_ram() includes. It does not change radius boundaries or metric definitions, and it does not make a hard radius smooth or remove concerns about local optima.

Map a metric

kernel_scale.raster() computes the same covariates for every raster cell. Projection of "sq", "ssk", "sku", "sdq", "sdr", and the landscape metrics uses fast Fourier transform (FFT) convolution by default. Unweighted "sa" uses an exact compiled moving-window pass instead, because average roughness cannot be written as a convolution. "sdq" and "sdr" use each cell's neighbors, so their projected values agree with point extraction to within a small tolerance at the buffer boundary rather than exactly. Set fft = FALSE in kernel_scale.raster() to use direct moving-window calculations instead.

References

Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. Landscape Ecology, 34(9), 2091-2101. doi:10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x

See also

kernel_prep(), multiScale_optim(), kernel_scale.raster(), and multiScaleR-kernels. For worked examples, see vignette("v04-landscape-metrics", package = "multiScaleR") for the landscape metrics and vignette("v05-surface-metrics", package = "multiScaleR") for the surface metrics.

Examples

## Kernel-weighted mean only (the same as omitting scale_vars)
vars <- msr_vars(forest_prop = kernel_var("forest"))
vars
#> multiScaleR variable specifications:
#>    covariate source   type metric radius optimize weighted     base classes_max
#>  forest_prop forest kernel   <NA>     NA     TRUE    FALSE 2.718282          NA
#>  class
#>     NA

## Combine kernel, landscape, and surface covariates. The printed table
## shows which scales are estimated (optimize = TRUE) and which are fixed.
vars <- msr_vars(
  forest_prop    = kernel_var("forest"),
  forest_ed      = landscape_var("forest", metric = "ed"),
  cover_shdi_500 = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "shdi", radius = 500),
  elev_sd        = surface_var("elevation", metric = "sq")
)
print(vars)
#> multiScaleR variable specifications:
#>       covariate    source      type metric radius optimize weighted     base

#>         elev_sd elevation   surface     sq     NA     TRUE    FALSE 2.718282

#>           NA    NA

## Compute covariates at survey points from the bundled landscape
land <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                                package = "multiScaleR"))
# land3 is continuous. Build a three-class layer from it
land$cover <- terra::classify(land$land3,
                              rbind(c(-Inf, 0.45, 1),
                                    c(0.45, 0.55, 2),
                                    c(0.55, Inf, 3)))
data("surv_pts")
vars <- msr_vars(
  land1_prop   = kernel_var("land1"),
  cover_shdi   = landscape_var("cover", metric = "shdi", radius = 400),
  land3_rough  = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 300)
)
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = terra::vect(surv_pts)[1:20, ],
                      raster_stack = land, max_D = 500,
                      scale_vars = vars, verbose = FALSE)
# Standardized covariates, one column per declared covariate
head(inputs$kernel_dat)
#>   land1_prop cover_shdi land3_rough
